questions.stem: Consider a processor that has 16 general purpose registers and it uses 2-byte instruction format for all its instructions. Variable-sized opcodes are permitted. There are three different types of instructions; M-type, R-type, and C-type. Each M-type instruction has 2 register operands and a 6-bit immediate operand. Each R-type instruction has 3 register operands. Each C-type instruction has a register operand and a 6-bit offset value. If there are 2 unique M-type opcodes and 7 unique R-type opcodes, which one of the following options gives the maximum number of unique opcodes possible for C-type instructions?

solutionDiagram.alt: Opcode space of the 16-bit format: 2-bit M opcodes, 4-bit R opcodes and 6-bit C opcodes, with 4 C-type opcodes left.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: An instruction is a string of bits, here 16 (2 bytes). The opcode field says which operation it is. A register field must name one of 16 registers, so it takes 4 bits. An immediate or offset is a number stored inside the instruction. Variable-sized opcodes mean each instruction type may spend a different number of bits on its opcode; the bits left over after the operands belong to the opcode. The decoder reads the instruction left to right, so no opcode may be the beginning of a longer one (the opcodes are prefix-free). That gives the rule: each unused short code can be extended by $k$ extra bits into $2^k$ longer codes, and a code that is used cannot be extended.

steps.title: Opcode width of each type
steps.body: M-type has two registers (8 bits) and 6 immediate bits, so the opcode has $16-8-6=2$ bits. R-type has three registers (12 bits), so the opcode has $16-12=4$ bits. C-type has one register (4 bits) and a 6-bit offset, so the opcode has $16-4-6=6$ bits. The more operand bits a type needs, the fewer bits its opcode gets, so the three widths are 2, 4 and 6.

steps.title: Spend the 2-bit codes on M-type
steps.body: There are $2^2=4$ two-bit codes and M-type uses 2 of them, leaving 2 unused. Each unused 2-bit code can be extended by 2 bits into $2^2=4$ four-bit codes, so $2\times4=8$ four-bit codes are available for R-type.

steps.title: Spend the 4-bit codes on R-type, then count C-type
steps.body: R-type uses 7 of the 8 four-bit codes, leaving 1. That one code extends by 2 bits into $2^{6-4}=4$ six-bit codes. These are the C-type opcodes. The maximum is 4, which is option B.

shortcut.body: Work down the levels, always (free codes) times 2 raised to the extra bits: $(4-2)\cdot4=8$, then $(8-7)\cdot4=4$. Opcode widths are 2, 4, 6, found by subtracting operand bits from 16. About two minutes; it is safe whenever the types are listed from short opcode to long opcode.

traps.text: The number 8 is the count of four-bit codes before the 7 R-type opcodes are taken away. Stopping one level early forgets that R-type uses most of them.
The number 64 is $2^6$, the whole six-bit space. It ignores that the M-type and R-type opcodes already use up prefixes of it.
The number 16 is $2^4$, the four-bit space taken as if M-type used none of it. The 2-bit M-type opcodes use half of the four-bit space.

recognize.clues: Variable-sized opcodes, three instruction types with different operand counts, and a fixed number of opcodes already given to two types while the question asks for the most the third can have.
recognize.contrast: A fixed-width opcode question just subtracts the operand bits and takes $2^k$. Here the widths differ by type, so unused short codes must be stretched into longer ones instead of counted directly.

check.body: Count in the 6-bit space instead of level by level. It holds 64 codes. Each 2-bit M-type opcode covers $2^4=16$ of them, so 2 of them cover 32. Each 4-bit R-type opcode covers $2^2=4$, so 7 of them cover 28. What is left is $64-32-28=4$.

hints.text: Each instruction type spends part of its 16 bits on operands. How many bits are left for the opcode in M-type, in R-type and in C-type?
Variable-sized opcodes form a prefix code: a short code that is taken as an opcode cannot also start a longer one, but a short code left unused can be stretched into several longer ones.
Each unused code at one width becomes $2^k$ codes at a width $k$ bits longer. Count what is free after the shorter types have taken their share, then stretch.
Get the three opcode widths from the operand bits. Then list how many codes exist at the shortest width, remove what the first type takes, and carry the rest forward to the next width.
At the shortest width there are 4 codes and the first type takes some of them. Stretch the leftovers to the next width and subtract the second type before moving on to the last width.

variation.stem: A processor has 16 general purpose registers and a 2-byte instruction format with variable-sized opcodes. Each M-type instruction has 2 register operands and a 6-bit immediate. Each R-type instruction has 3 register operands. Each C-type instruction has 1 register operand and a 6-bit offset. There is 1 M-type opcode and 5 R-type opcodes. What is the maximum number of unique opcodes possible for C-type instructions?
variation.explanation: The opcode widths are 2, 4 and 6 bits. The 2-bit space has 4 codes, 1 goes to M-type, and the other 3 stretch into $3\cdot4=12$ four-bit codes. R-type takes 5, leaving 7, and these stretch into $7\cdot4=28$ six-bit codes for C-type. Option A stops one level early, B forgets the M-type opcode, and D forgets to remove the R-type opcodes.

questions.stem: Match each addressing mode in List I with a data element or an element of a data structure (in a high-level language) in List II:

steps.title: What an addressing mode is
steps.body: An addressing mode is the rule that turns the operand field of an instruction into the operand itself. Four rules matter here. Immediate: the field is the value. Indirect: the field is the address of a memory word that holds the address of the operand. Base with index: the address is a base register plus an index register. Base with offset: the address is a base register plus a constant written in the instruction. Each rule fits one shape of high-level data, and the question asks which.

steps.title: Match by what the rule can express
steps.body: Immediate stores the value inside the instruction, so it can only express a constant: P to 4. Indirect reaches the operand through a stored address, which is exactly what a pointer variable is: Q to 2. Base with index adds a changing register to a fixed array base, so stepping the index walks over array elements: R to 1. Base with offset adds a fixed constant to a base register that holds the start of a record, and the constant picks the field: S to 3.

steps.title: Choose the option
steps.body: The pairing P-4, Q-2, R-1, S-3 is option B.

shortcut.body: Fix the two certain pairs first: immediate is a constant (4) and indirect is a pointer (2). Only option B has both. Ten seconds.

traps.text: Swapping Q and S, so indirect is read as a record field and displacement as a pointer. Indirect means one more memory hop, which is what following a pointer does.
Calling immediate an array element. An immediate value is fixed in the instruction text, so it cannot change from one element to the next.
Calling immediate a pointer and pairing S with a constant. A displacement is a constant that is added to an address, but the thing it reaches is a field, not the constant itself.

recognize.clues: The question lists four named modes and four high-level data shapes (constant, pointer, array element, record field), so the task is to say which shape each mode can express.
recognize.contrast: Base with index and base with offset both add to a base register. The index is a register that changes between passes, so it walks an array; the offset is a constant inside the instruction, so it selects a fixed field.

check.body: Count memory reads for one use of each shape. A constant needs none, because the value is in the instruction. A pointer needs two: read the pointer, then read what it points to. An array element and a record field each need one, after an address is formed with a changing index or a fixed offset. Only immediate and indirect match the zero and two counts, which fixes the first two pairs independently of the other two.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: gate cse 2026 set 1 question 4
GATE 2026 CS-1 answer key, IIT Guwahati (organising institute)

hints.text: For each mode, ask what the operand field holds: the value itself, an address, or a part that is added to a register. Then ask which data shape needs exactly that.
Indirect addressing adds one hop. The field names a memory word, and that word holds the address of the operand.

For each mode, ask how often the part you can vary is allowed to change: never, on every pass of a loop, or only when the instruction is written. The mode suits whatever program data behaves the same way.
Settle the two modes you are sure of first, then use them to drop options, and only then sort the two modes that both add to a base register.
Between the two base modes, ask which one has an addend that moves while a loop runs and which one has an addend that is written once into the instruction.

variation.stem: Match each addressing mode in List I with the high-level construct in List II that it suits best. List I: P. Auto-increment, Q. Base with offset/displacement, R. Immediate, S. Register indirect. List II: 1. Visiting array elements one after another, 2. Field of a record, 3. Literal constant in an expression, 4. Pointer held in a register.
variation.explanation: Auto-increment moves the address on after each use, which is exactly a walk over an array: P to 1. A displacement is a fixed offset from a base register, which picks a field: Q to 2. Immediate holds the value in the instruction, a literal: R to 3. Register indirect uses a register as the address, which is a pointer: S to 4.

questions.stem: Consider a processor P whose instruction set architecture is the load-store architecture. The instruction format is such that the first operand of any instruction is the destination operand. Which one of the following sequences of instructions corresponds to the high-level language statement Z = X + Y? Note: X, Y, and Z are memory operands. R0, R1, and R2 are registers.
options:
LOAD R0, X
ADD Z, R0, Y

ADD R0, X, Y
STORE Z, R0

LOAD R0, X
LOAD R1, Y
ADD R2, R0, R1
STORE Z, R2

steps.title: Load-store architecture
steps.body: A load-store architecture lets only two kinds of instruction touch memory: LOAD (memory to register) and STORE (register to memory). Every other instruction, such as ADD, takes registers only. The statement says the first operand is the destination, so ADD R2, R0, R1 means R2 = R0 + R1, and STORE Z, R2 writes R2 into Z. The rule that decides the question: any ADD with a memory name is illegal.

steps.title: Test each option
steps.body: Option A adds with three memory operands. Option B puts memory name Z as the destination of ADD and memory Y as a source. Option C reads X and Y straight from memory inside ADD. Option D loads X into R0, loads Y into R1, adds them into R2 with registers only, and stores R2 into Z. Only D obeys the rule, and it computes Z = X + Y.

shortcut.body: Scan for ADD lines that mention X, Y or Z. A, B and C all have one; D does not. Fifteen seconds.

traps.text: This is a memory-to-memory three-address ADD, valid on a CISC machine but not on a load-store machine.
Half the work is done through registers, but ADD still names the memory operands Z and Y, so it breaks the rule.
The STORE is correct but ADD reads X and Y from memory directly. The load instructions are missing.

recognize.clues: The wording says load-store architecture and that X, Y and Z are memory operands while R0 to R2 are registers, so the test is where each operand of each instruction may live.
recognize.contrast: A memory-to-memory three-address machine (CISC style) can add directly from memory in one instruction. Load-store separates moving data from computing, which is why more instructions are needed here.

check.body: Trace values. Let X be 3 and Y be 4. Option D sets R0 to 3, R1 to 4, R2 to 7 and stores 7 into Z. Every instruction touches memory only through LOAD or STORE. Each other option contains an ADD that names a memory operand, which a load-store machine cannot encode at all.

hints.text: Look at what each ADD names as its operands. Is an arithmetic instruction allowed to name something that lives in memory on this machine?
In a load-store architecture only LOAD and STORE reach memory. Every other instruction works on registers alone.
A sequence is valid only if every arithmetic instruction uses registers, each memory value is brought in by a LOAD first, and the result is written back by a STORE.
Decide which of X, Y and Z must be in registers when the add executes, and how the sum gets back into memory. Then see which option does exactly that.

variation.stem: A load-store processor writes the destination operand first, and SUB Rd, Rs1, Rs2 means Rd = Rs1 - Rs2. X, Y and Z are memory operands and R0, R1 and R2 are registers. Which one of the following sequences computes Z = X - Y?
options:
LOAD R0, X
LOAD R1, Y
SUB R2, R1, R0
STORE Z, R2

LOAD R0, X
LOAD R1, Y
SUB R2, R0, R1
STORE Z, R2

LOAD R0, X
SUB R1, R0, Y
STORE Z, R1
variation.explanation: Both values must be loaded into registers, the subtraction must use registers only, and the result must be stored. Option C subtracts in the right order, $R0-R1=X-Y$. Option B is also register-only but computes $Y-X$, A and D name memory inside SUB.

questions.stem: Which of the following is/are part of an Instruction Set Architecture of a processor?
options: The size of the cache memory
The clock frequency of the processor
The number of cache memory levels

steps.title: ISA versus implementation
steps.body: The Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) is the contract between hardware and a programmer: the instructions, their encodings, the addressing modes, the data types and the programmer-visible registers. Anything a program can name or depend on for correctness belongs to it. The microarchitecture is how one chip meets that contract: cache sizes, pipeline depth, clock speed. Two chips with different microarchitecture can share one ISA and run the same binary.

steps.title: Sort the four statements
steps.body: Cache size and number of cache levels change speed, not what any instruction means, so they belong to the implementation (A and C are out). Clock frequency is also implementation (B is out). The number of registers decides which register names an instruction can use and how wide the register fields are, so it is part of the ISA (D is in). The answer is D only.

shortcut.body: Ask whether a compiler needs the item to generate correct code. Registers: yes. Cache size, cache levels and clock: no, they only change speed. Fifteen seconds.

traps.text: Cache size is invisible to the instruction set; software runs the same, only faster or slower.
Clock frequency sets speed and belongs to the implementation, not to the architecture.
The cache hierarchy is transparent to programs, so the number of levels is not an architectural choice.

recognize.clues: The wording asks what is part of the Instruction Set Architecture, and the options mix speed and capacity features (cache, clock) with a programmer-visible resource.
recognize.contrast: Instruction set architecture is the programmer-visible contract; microarchitecture is the implementation behind it. Cache, clock and pipeline depth are implementation, while registers, instructions and addressing modes are contract.

check.body: Run the swap test on each item. A 64 KB cache against a 1 MB cache, or 2 GHz against 3 GHz, gives the same results from the same binary, only faster. A chip with fewer registers than the code names would reject or misread the program. Only the item that can break a binary is architectural.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: gate cse 2025 set 2 question 18
GATE 2025 CS-2 final answer key, IIT Roorkee (organising institute)

hints.text: For each item, ask whether a compiler writer or an assembly programmer must know it to produce a correct program.
The ISA is the visible interface between software and hardware. Microarchitecture is how one particular chip delivers that interface.
An item belongs to the ISA when changing it can change which programs are valid or what an instruction means. It does not belong when only the run time changes.
Take the items one at a time and imagine two chips that differ only in that item. Ask whether the same binary would still run correctly on both.

variation.stem: Which of the following is/are part of the Instruction Set Architecture of a processor?
options: The set of addressing modes the instructions support
The width of a general purpose register
The access time of main memory
variation.explanation: Apply the swap test: could the same binary behave differently on two chips that differ only in this item? Addressing modes decide what instructions mean, and register width decides what values a program can hold, so both are architectural. Pipeline depth and memory access time change only speed.

questions.stem: A processor has 64 general-purpose registers and 50 distinct instruction types. An instruction is encoded in 32-bits. What is the maximum number of bits that can be used to store the immediate operand for the given instruction?

solutionDiagram.alt: The 32-bit ADD format split into a 6-bit opcode, a 6-bit register and a 20-bit immediate.

steps.title: Fields and the rule
steps.body: An instruction word is a fixed number of bits cut into fields. The opcode names the operation, so with $n$ distinct instruction types it needs $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ bits. A register field names one of $r$ registers and needs $\lceil\log_2 r\rceil$ bits. The immediate is a number kept inside the word. Everything that is not opcode or register is free for the immediate, so its maximum size is the word size minus the other fields.

steps.title: Size each field
steps.body: Opcode: 50 types need $\lceil\log_2 50\rceil=6$ bits, since $2^5=32<50\le64$. Register: 64 registers need 6 bits. The instruction ADD R1, #25 has one register operand and one immediate.

steps.title: Subtract
steps.body: Immediate bits $=32-6-6=20$, which is option B.

shortcut.body: Opcode 6, register 6, so $32-12=20$. Check that 50 is between 32 and 64 to get 6, not 5. Thirty seconds.

traps.text: Treating fields as whole bytes (an 8-bit opcode and an 8-bit register) leaves 16 bits. Fields are sized to the bit, not rounded up to bytes.
Giving the register only 4 bits (confusing 64 registers with 16) and the opcode 6 gives 22. 64 registers need 6 bits.
Dropping the register field and keeping a byte-wide opcode gives 24. The instruction names R1, so the register field is needed.

recognize.clues: A fixed instruction width, a register count, an instruction-type count, and a question about the most bits left for one operand field.
recognize.contrast: In the expanding-opcode kind of question the opcode width differs by type and unused codes are stretched. Here one opcode width serves every instruction, so the sizes are simply subtracted.

check.body: Add the fields back: opcode, register and immediate must fill the word exactly. They do, with nothing spare. Then try one more immediate bit: the other two fields would have only 11 bits, but the opcode alone needs enough for 50 types and the register needs enough for 64 registers, and these cannot fit in 11.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: gate cse 2025 set 1 question 27
GATE 2025 CS-1 final answer key, IIT Roorkee (organising institute)

hints.text: The 32-bit word is fully divided into fields. Which fields does ADD R1, #25 need, and which one are you asked to make as large as possible?
A field that must tell $n$ things apart needs enough bits for $n$ different patterns, and the bit count is always a whole number.
Everything not used by the opcode and the register field is free, so the largest immediate is the word size minus those fields.
Get the opcode bits from the number of instruction types and the bits of one register field from the register count. Then write the word as opcode, register, immediate.
To size the opcode, place 50 between two neighbouring powers of two and take the larger exponent. The register count is already a power of two.

variation.stem: A processor has 128 general-purpose registers and 100 distinct instruction types. An instruction is encoded in 48 bits. The instruction ADD R1, #25 has one register operand and one immediate. What is the maximum number of bits that can be used to store the immediate operand?
variation.explanation: The opcode needs $\lceil\log_2 100\rceil=7$ bits since $64<100\le128$, and the register needs $\log_2 128=7$ bits. The immediate gets $48-7-7=34$ bits. Option A rounds the opcode down to 6, B drops the register field, and D rounds both fields up to whole bytes.

questions.stem: A processor with 16 general purpose registers uses a 32-bit instruction format. The instruction format consists of an opcode field, an addressing mode field, two register operand fields, and a 16-bit scalar field. If 8 addressing modes are to be supported, the maximum number of unique opcodes possible for every addressing mode is _________

solutionDiagram.alt: The 32-bit format: 5-bit opcode, 3-bit addressing mode, two 4-bit register fields and a 16-bit scalar.

steps.title: Fields and what the question counts
steps.body: The instruction word has 32 bits split into five fields: opcode, addressing mode, two register operands and a 16-bit scalar. A field of $k$ bits can hold $2^k$ different values. The question asks how many different opcode values the opcode field can hold; since the addressing mode sits in its own field, every mode can be combined with every opcode value.

steps.title: Size the other fields
steps.body: Eight addressing modes need $\log_2 8=3$ bits. Each register field names one of 16 registers and takes 4 bits, so two take 8 bits. The scalar takes 16 bits. These add up to $3+8+16=27$ bits.

steps.title: Opcode bits and count
steps.body: The opcode gets what is left, $32-27=5$ bits, so it holds $2^5=32$ values. Each of the 8 modes can be used with all 32.

shortcut.body: Add the fixed fields, $3+4+4+16=27$, so the opcode has 5 bits and $2^5=32$. Do not divide by the number of modes. About one minute.

traps.text: Dividing the 32 opcodes among the 8 modes gives 4. The mode is its own field, so each mode can use the whole opcode set.
Forgetting the 3-bit mode field leaves 8 opcode bits and 256. The mode field must be subtracted.
Counting only one register field (4 bits) leaves 9 opcode bits and 512. The format has two register fields.

recognize.clues: A fixed 32-bit format with named fields (opcode, mode, two registers, scalar) and a question that asks for how many opcode values fit.
recognize.contrast: Do not treat the modes as sharing the opcode values. In a separate-field format every mode combines with every opcode value; in an encoding where the mode is folded into the opcode, the values would be divided.

check.body: Work backwards from the result. A 5-bit opcode, a 3-bit mode, two 4-bit registers and a 16-bit scalar total 32 bits with nothing spare. A 6-bit opcode would need 33 bits, so it cannot fit, and a 4-bit opcode would leave a bit unused.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: gate cse 2024 set 2 question 47
GATE 2024 CS2 final answer key (organising institute IISc Bengaluru), GATE archive copy on the IIT Guwahati site

hints.text: The opcode is whatever remains of the 32 bits once every other field is sized. List the other fields first.
A field of $k$ bits holds $2^k$ different values, so $n$ choices need $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ bits.
The addressing mode has its own field, so it costs bits but does not split the opcode values among modes.
Find the bits of the mode field from the number of modes and of one register field from the register count, add the register fields and the scalar, and take the remainder for the opcode.
Two register fields at 4 bits each take 8 bits. Add the mode field and the scalar to that total before you subtract from the word size.

variation.stem: A processor with 8 general purpose registers uses a 24-bit instruction format. The format consists of an opcode field, an addressing mode field, two register operand fields and a 10-bit scalar field. If 4 addressing modes are to be supported, the maximum number of unique opcodes possible for every addressing mode is _________
variation.explanation: The mode field needs $\log_2 4=2$ bits, each register field needs $\log_2 8=3$ bits, and the scalar has 10 bits, so the other fields use $2+6+10=18$ bits. The opcode has $24-18=6$ bits and holds $2^6=64$ values, each usable with every mode.

questions.stem: A processor uses a 32-bit instruction format and supports byte-addressable memory access. The ISA of the processor has 150 distinct instructions. The instructions are equally divided into two types, namely R-type and I-type, whose formats are shown below. In the OPCODE, 1 bit is used to distinguish between I-type and R-type instructions and the remaining bits indicate the operation. The processor has 50 architectural registers, and all register fields in the instructions are of equal size. Let $X$ be the number of bits used to encode the UNUSED field, $Y$ be the number of bits used to encode the OPCODE field, and $Z$ be the number of bits used to encode the immediate value/address field. The value of $X + 2Y + Z$ is ________

rows: OPCODE, UNUSED, DST Register, SRC Register 1, SRC Register 2
OPCODE, DST Register, SRC Register, # Immediate value/address

solutionDiagram.alt: The R-type and I-type 32-bit formats with an 8-bit opcode, 6-bit register fields, a 6-bit UNUSED field and a 12-bit immediate.

steps.title: Fields and the sizing rule
steps.body: Both formats fill exactly 32 bits. An opcode that must tell $n$ operations apart needs $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ bits; a register field that names one of $r$ registers needs $\lceil\log_2 r\rceil$ bits. The UNUSED field and the immediate take whatever bits remain after the opcode and register fields.

steps.title: Opcode and register widths
steps.body: The 150 instructions are split equally: 75 R-type and 75 I-type. One opcode bit tells the type, and the rest must tell 75 operations apart: $\lceil\log_2 75\rceil=7$ bits since $64<75\le128$. So $Y=1+7=8$. The 50 registers need $\lceil\log_2 50\rceil=6$ bits for every register field.

steps.title: The leftover fields
steps.body: R-type has three register fields: $X=32-8-3\cdot6=6$. I-type has two register fields: $Z=32-8-2\cdot6=12$. Then $X+2Y+Z=6+16+12=34$.

shortcut.body: Opcode 8, register 6. R-type: $32-8-18=6$. I-type: $32-8-12=12$. Total $6+16+12=34$. The opcode width cancels, because $X+Z=64-2Y-5r$, so the total is $64-5r=34$ with $r=6$. Two minutes.

traps.text: Rounding $\log_2 50\approx5.6$ down to 5 bits per register gives $X=9$, $Z=14$ and $9+16+14=39$. A field must hold every register number, so round up to 6.
Giving R-type only two register fields instead of three (the UNUSED field is separate from DST, SRC1, SRC2) gives $X=12$ and a total of 40.
Dropping the factor 2 on $Y$ and computing $X+Y+Z=6+8+12$ gives 26. Read the expression exactly as printed.

recognize.clues: Two named formats of the same 32-bit width, equal-size register fields, one opcode bit that selects the type, and a combined expression of the leftover fields.
recognize.contrast: This is not an expanding-opcode question. The opcode has the same width in both formats, so the leftovers are plain subtraction per format.

check.body: Add each format back to 32. R-type holds an 8-bit opcode, the UNUSED field, and three 6-bit registers. I-type holds the 8-bit opcode, two 6-bit registers and the immediate. Both sums reach 32 bits exactly only with the fields found, which confirms that the two leftover widths are consistent with one opcode width and one register width.

GATE 2024 CS2 final answer key (organising institute IISc Bengaluru), GATE archive copy on the IIT Guwahati site

hints.text: You need X, Y and Z separately, so first work out the width of the opcode and of one register field.
The opcode must tell the operations apart, and here it also carries one extra bit that tells the two instruction types apart.
Each format fills the 32 bits exactly, so UNUSED and the immediate are whatever remains in their own format after the opcode and the register fields.
Count the register fields in each format. They differ between R-type and I-type, and UNUSED exists only in one of them.
The 150 instructions are split equally between the two types, so each type has its own count of operations. Take the bits for that count and add the type bit to get the opcode width.

variation.stem: A processor uses a 32-bit instruction format. Its ISA has 100 distinct instructions, equally divided into R-type and I-type. In the opcode, 1 bit tells I-type from R-type and the remaining bits indicate the operation. The processor has 20 architectural registers, and all register fields are of equal size. An R-type instruction has the fields OPCODE, UNUSED, DST, SRC1, SRC2. An I-type instruction has OPCODE, DST, SRC, IMMEDIATE. Let $X$ be the number of bits in UNUSED, $Y$ the bits in OPCODE and $Z$ the bits in IMMEDIATE. The value of $X + 2Y + Z$ is ________
variation.explanation: Each type has 50 operations, so the opcode takes $1+\lceil\log_2 50\rceil=7$ bits, and 20 registers need 5 bits per register field. Then $X=32-7-15=10$ and $Z=32-7-10=15$. The total is $10+14+15=39$.

questions.stem: Consider the given C-code and its corresponding assembly code, with a few operands U1–U4 being unknown. Some useful information as well as the semantics of each unique assembly instruction is annotated as inline comments in the code. The memory is byte-addressable. Which one of the following options is a CORRECT replacement for operands in the position (U1, U2, U3, U4) in the above assembly code?

code.text:
//C-code                    ;assembly-code (; indicates comments)
                            ;r1-r5 are 32-bit integer registers
                            ;initialize r1=0, r2=10
                            ;initialize r3, r4 with base address of a, b

int a[10], b[10], i;        L01: jeq r1, r2, end ;if(r1==r2) goto end
// int is 32-bit           L02: lw r5, 0(r4)        ;r5 <- Memory[r4+0]
for (i=0; i<10;i++)         L03: shl r5, r5, U1      ;r5 <- r5 << U1
    a[i] = b[i] * 8;        L04: sw r5, 0(r3)        ;Memory[r3+0] <- r5
                            L05: add r3, r3, U2      ;r3 <- r3+U2
                            L06: add r4, r4, U3
                            L07: add r1, r1, 1
                            L08: jmp U4              ;goto U4
                            L09: end

solutionDiagram.alt: Array b in memory: 4-byte int elements, so the pointer registers advance by 4 each pass.

steps.title: Byte addressing and shifts
steps.body: In a byte-addressable memory every address names one byte. A 32-bit int occupies 4 bytes, so element $i$ of an int array starts at base $+4i$, and moving from one element to the next adds 4 to the address. A left shift by $k$ multiplies by $2^k$, so multiplying by 8 is a shift by 3. The jump at the bottom of a loop returns to the test at the top.

steps.title: Fill the four blanks
steps.body: U1: b[i]*8 is a shift left by 3, so $U1=3$ (shifting by 8 would multiply by $2^8$). U2: r3 walks over a, and the next int is 4 bytes on, so $U2=4$. U3: r4 walks over b the same way, $U3=4$. U4: after the increment the loop must test again whether r1 equals r2, so the jump goes to L01. Jumping to L02 would skip the test and load past the end of b.

steps.title: Match the option
steps.body: Option B is (3, 4, 4, L01). Run it: ten passes, r3 and r4 each move $10\times4=40$ bytes, every a[i] gets 8 times b[i], and the loop leaves at L01 when r1 reaches 10.

shortcut.body: Shift for times 8 is 3; int steps are 4 bytes; a loop jumps back to its test. Only B has 3, 4, 4, L01. Thirty seconds.

traps.text: Using 8 as the shift amount confuses the multiplier with the shift count, and U2 = 4 with U3 = 1 moves b by one byte per pass.
A shift of 8 multiplies by 256, and a step of 1 byte reads the middle of an int, not the next element.
The shift 3 and the target L01 are right, but pointer steps of 1 move only a byte at a time. Pointer steps equal the element size, 4.

recognize.clues: The memory is byte-addressable, the arrays hold 32-bit ints, the source multiplies by a power of 2, and the pointers are advanced by hand each pass.
recognize.contrast: Scaled indexing would multiply the index by the element size automatically. Here the program does the scaling itself by adding the element size to each pointer, so the byte step must be written out.

check.body: Trace two passes with b at address 100 and a at address 200. After the first pass r4 is 104 and r3 is 204, which are the starts of the second ints. Steps of 1 would leave both pointers inside the first int. Also check the shift: shifting 5 left by 3 gives 40, which is $5\times8$.

questions.stem: Consider the following instruction sequence where registers R1, R2 and R3 are general purpose and MEMORY[X] denotes the content at the memory location X. Assume that the content of the memory location 5000 is 10, and the content of the register R3 is 3000. The content of each of the memory locations from 3000 to 3010 is 50. The instruction sequence starts from the memory location 1000. All the numbers are in decimal format. Assume that the memory is byte addressable. After the execution of the program, the content of memory location 3010 is ________.

rows: Branch if not zero to the given absolute address

solutionDiagram.alt: The program listing from address 1000 with a loop arrow from BNZ at 1018 back to 1004, run 10 times.

steps.title: Reading the instruction set
steps.body: This is a trace question: run the program by hand and keep every register and memory cell that changes. Parentheses mean "the memory cell at that address", so MOV R1,(5000) reads memory, and MOV (R3),R2 writes memory. Because memory is byte-addressable and instructions have different sizes, the next address is the current address plus the current size. BNZ jumps when the last tested register, R1 after DEC R1, is not zero.

steps.title: Addresses of the instructions
steps.body: From 1000: MOV R1 (4 bytes) at 1000, MOV R2 at 1004, ADD at 1008, MOV (R3),R2 at 1010, INC R3 at 1014, DEC R1 at 1016, BNZ at 1018, HALT at 1020. BNZ 1004 therefore jumps to the second instruction, so R1 is loaded only once, before the loop.

steps.title: What one pass does
steps.body: Pass $k$ (starting at 0) has R1 $=10-k$ and R3 $=3000+k$. It reads MEMORY[3000+k] (50), adds R1, writes the sum back, adds 1 to R3 and subtracts 1 from R1. So MEMORY[3000+k] becomes $50+(10-k)$.

steps.title: When it stops
steps.body: After pass $k$, R1 $=9-k$, so BNZ loops back until R1 hits 0 after pass 9. That is 10 passes, writing locations 3000 to 3009. R3 ends at 3010, but R3 is incremented after the write, so MEMORY[3010] is read by no pass and written by none. It keeps its starting value, 50.

shortcut.body: Count the writes: R1 starts at 10 and BNZ exits when it reaches 0, so 10 passes write 3000 to 3009. Address 3010 is the one past the end, so it stays 50. Check that INC R3 comes after the store. Two minutes.

traps.text: Letting R3 start at 3001 instead of 3000. The pointer is then one cell ahead, so pass 9 writes 3010 while R1 is 1, giving 51. The loop count is still set by R1 from 10 down to 0, which gives 10 passes starting at 3000.
Answering 51 or 60 by assuming the last write lands on 3010. R3 reaches 3010 only after the final store.
Treating BNZ 1004 as a jump back to 1000, which would reload R1 as 10 every pass and never terminate.

recognize.clues: A listed program with register-indirect loads and stores, a loop closed by BNZ, and a question about the value of one memory cell after the program ends.
recognize.contrast: A plain addressing-mode question asks for one effective address. Here the same indirect store repeats with a moving pointer, so you keep a table of register and cell values pass by pass.

check.body: Replay only the final pass. It starts with R1 at 1 and R3 at 3009, stores into 3009, then INC makes R3 equal 3010 and DEC makes R1 zero. BNZ is not taken, HALT runs, and no store ever used the address 3010.
check.tex: \text{last store at } 3009,\ R3\text{ reaches }3010\text{ only afterwards}

questions.stem: A processor has 64 registers and uses 16-bit instruction format. It has two types of instructions: I-type and R-type. Each I-type instruction contains an opcode, a register name, and a 4-bit immediate value. Each R-type instruction contains an opcode and two register names. If there are 8 distinct I-type opcodes, then the maximum number of distinct R-type opcodes is ______.

solutionDiagram.alt: Opcode space of the 16-bit format: 8 six-bit I-type opcodes use 2 of 16 four-bit prefixes, leaving 14 for R-type.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: The 16 bits are cut into an opcode and operand fields. A register name must pick one of 64 registers, so it takes 6 bits. An immediate of 4 bits is just 4 bits of the word. The opcode gets what the operands leave over, so the two types have opcodes of different length. The decoder reads from the left, so no short opcode may be the beginning of a longer one. Using a short code up uses all longer codes that begin with it: one 4-bit code covers $2^{6-4}=4$ six-bit codes.

steps.title: Opcode widths
steps.body: I-type: one register (6 bits) and a 4-bit immediate leave $16-6-4=6$ bits for the opcode. R-type: two registers (12 bits) leave $16-12=4$ bits for the opcode.

steps.title: Count the prefixes
steps.body: There are $2^4=16$ four-bit codes. The 8 I-type opcodes are six-bit codes, and each four-bit code covers 4 of them, so $8/4=2$ four-bit codes are taken (any other choice only wastes space). The remaining $16-2=14$ four-bit codes are free for R-type.

shortcut.body: Opcodes are 6 bits and 4 bits. Eight six-bit codes fill $8/4=2$ four-bit prefixes, so $16-2=14$. A minute. The shortcut needs the number of I-type opcodes to be a multiple of 4; otherwise round up before subtracting.

traps.text: Subtracting the 8 I-type opcodes straight from 16 gives 8. The I-type codes are longer, so each one uses only a quarter of a four-bit code.
Subtracting 8 from 64 gives 56. That mixes the six-bit space with the four-bit R-type opcode field.
Saying 16 because the R-type opcode field has 4 bits. The I-type opcodes use up part of that space.

recognize.clues: Two instruction types of different operand sizes in one fixed 16-bit word, a given number of opcodes for one type, and a request for the largest number for the other type.
recognize.contrast: Computing field widths for a single format only needs powers of two. Here two formats share the opcode space, so the short codes left depend on how many long codes were already placed.

check.body: Count in the 6-bit space, which holds 64 codes. The 8 I-type opcodes take 8 of them. Each 4-bit R-type opcode is the prefix of 4 six-bit codes, so it uses up 4 of them, which bounds the R-type count by the quotient below.

One unused short code can be split into $2^k$ longer codes by adding $k$ bits. Long codes therefore use up short codes in whole groups.
Find the two opcode widths. Count all codes of the shorter width, then work out how many of them the longer I-type opcodes must claim, rounding up to whole short codes.

variation.stem: A processor has 32 registers and a 16-bit instruction. An I-type instruction holds an opcode, one register name and a 3-bit immediate. An R-type instruction holds an opcode and two register names. There are 12 distinct I-type opcodes. What is the maximum number of distinct R-type opcodes?
variation.explanation: A register name takes 5 bits, so the I-type opcode has $16-5-3=8$ bits and the R-type opcode has $16-10=6$ bits. There are $2^6=64$ six-bit codes. Each 8-bit I-type code is a quarter of a six-bit code, so 12 of them occupy $12/4=3$ six-bit codes, leaving $64-3=61$.

questions.stem: Consider the following processor design characteristics. I. Register-to-register arithmetic operations only. II. Fixed-length instruction format. III. Hardwired control unit. Which of the characteristics above are used in the design of a RISC processor?

steps.title: What RISC means
steps.body: RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) keeps the instruction set small and regular so that the hardware can be simple and fast. Its design rules are: arithmetic works on registers only and memory is reached by separate load and store instructions; every instruction has the same length so that fetch and decode are easy; and because each instruction is simple, the control unit is hardwired (built from gates) instead of microprogrammed. CISC machines do the opposite on all three.

steps.title: Check the three characteristics
steps.body: I is the load-store rule of RISC. II is the fixed-length rule. III is standard in RISC designs, since simple instructions do not need a control store. All three hold, so the answer is "I, II and III", option D.

shortcut.body: Recall the three RISC marks: load-store, fixed length, hardwired control. All three are listed, so D. Ten seconds.

traps.text: Leaving out the hardwired control unit. RISC designers choose hardwired control because their simple instructions need no microcode.
Leaving out register-to-register arithmetic. That is the defining load-store feature of RISC.
Leaving out fixed-length instructions. Uniform length is what lets RISC decode in one step and pipeline cleanly.

recognize.clues: The question lists design characteristics of a processor and asks which of them belong to a RISC design, with no numbers to compute.
recognize.contrast: The look-alike is the CISC list: memory operands in arithmetic, variable instruction length and microprogrammed control. Compare each statement with that list to tell the two styles apart.

check.body: Test the opposite design. A CISC machine allows memory operands in arithmetic, mixes instruction lengths and often uses microcode, so each of the three statements is the reverse of a CISC property. Properties that reverse CISC on every point fit RISC on every point.

questions.stem: A processor has 16 integer registers (R0, R1, .. , R15) and 64 floating point registers (F0, F1,… , F63). It uses a 2-byte instruction format. There are four categories of instructions: Type-1, Type-2, Type-3, and Type-4. Type-1 category consists of four instructions, each with 3 integer register operands (3Rs). Type-2 category consists of eight instructions, each with 2 floating point register operands (2Fs). Type-3 category consists of fourteen instructions, each with one integer register operand and one floating point register operand (1R+1F). Type-4 category consists of N instructions, each with a floating point register operand (1F). The maximum value of N is __________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Opcode space of the 2-byte format: Type-1 and Type-2 use 12 of 16 four-bit codes, Type-3 uses 14 of 16 grown six-bit codes, leaving 32 ten-bit codes.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: The instruction is 16 bits. Each type has an opcode plus register fields; an integer register needs 4 bits (16 registers) and a floating point register needs 6 bits (64 registers). The opcode takes the bits left over, so the types have opcodes of different lengths. The decoder reads from the left, so a code in use by one type may not be the beginning of another type's opcode. An unused code of length $a$ can be grown into $2^{b-a}$ codes of length $b$.

steps.title: Opcode length for each type
steps.body: Type-1: three integer registers use 12 bits, so the opcode has $16-12=4$ bits. Type-2: two floating registers use 12 bits, so 4 bits. Type-3: 4 + 6 = 10 bits of operands, so 6 bits. Type-4: one floating register uses 6 bits, so the opcode has 10 bits.

steps.title: Spend the four-bit codes
steps.body: There are $2^4=16$ four-bit codes. Type-1 uses 4 and Type-2 uses 8, leaving $16-12=4$. Each grows into $2^{6-4}=4$ six-bit codes, which gives 16.

steps.title: Spend the six-bit codes, then count Type-4
steps.body: Type-3 uses 14 of those 16 six-bit codes, leaving 2. Each grows into $2^{10-6}=16$ ten-bit codes, so $N_{\max}=2\times16=32$.

shortcut.body: Opcode lengths are 4, 4, 6, 10. Chain the free counts: $(16-4-8)\cdot4=16$; $(16-14)\cdot16=32$. Two to three minutes; draw the levels so you do not skip one.

traps.text: Stopping at the six-bit level and answering 2 (the free six-bit codes) forgets that Type-4 opcodes are 10 bits and each free code expands 16 times.
Expanding only one of the two spare six-bit codes gives 16. Both spare codes are free to use.
Giving the floating point register 4 bits (as for integer registers) changes every opcode length and lands on a wrong count. 64 registers need 6 bits.

recognize.clues: A fixed 2-byte word, four instruction categories whose register operands cost different numbers of bits, and a request for the largest count in the last category.
recognize.contrast: A single-format question only needs $2^{\text{opcode bits}}$. Here four formats share one opcode space, so the free codes have to be extended level by level.

check.body: Count in the 10-bit space, which holds 1024 codes. A 4-bit opcode covers $2^6=64$ of them, a 6-bit opcode covers $2^4=16$, and a 10-bit opcode covers 1. Subtract what Types 1, 2 and 3 cover and see what is left for Type-4.

variation.stem: A processor has 8 integer registers and 32 floating point registers and uses a 2-byte instruction. Type-A has 6 instructions, each with 2 floating point register operands. Type-B has 5 instructions, each with 3 integer register operands. Type-C has 20 instructions, each with one integer and one floating point register operand. questions.stem: Consider the C struct defined below: The base address of student is available in register R1. The field student.grade can be accessed efficiently using
options: Index addressing mode, X(R1), where X is an offset represented in 2’s complement 16-bit representation.

solutionDiagram.alt: Layout of struct data: marks takes bytes 0 to 399, grade is at byte 400, so X(R1) with X = 400 reaches it.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: A struct stores its fields one after another in memory, each at a fixed distance (offset) from the start of the struct. Index (displacement) addressing X(R1) forms the address R1 + X: R1 holds a base address, and the constant X inside the instruction is the offset. That is exactly what reaching a field of a record needs, a base plus a fixed constant.

steps.title: Find the field
steps.body: marks takes $100\times4=400$ bytes, so grade starts at offset 400. The base of student is in R1, so the address of student.grade is R1 + 400. The instruction can carry X = 400 as a signed 16-bit number (range $-32768$ to $32767$), so index mode X(R1) reaches the field in one operand.

steps.title: Rule out the others
steps.body: Post-increment (R1)+ and pre-decrement –(R1) use R1 as the address and change R1 by the operand size; they would reach marks[0] or the bytes before the struct, not offset 400. Register direct R1 names the register content as the operand, which is the base address value, not a field. Only D is right.

shortcut.body: A struct field is base plus constant offset, which is displacement/index mode X(R1). Ten seconds.

traps.text: Post-increment reads from R1 itself, which is the address of marks[0], and then moves R1 on by the operand size. It never adds the offset 400.
Pre-decrement first moves R1 back and reads the memory before the struct. Either way it does not add a field offset.
Register direct uses the content of R1 as the operand itself, not as an address, so it gives the base address and no memory access.

recognize.clues: A struct whose base address is held in a register, with a field that lies after a known array, so the address needed is the base plus a constant.
recognize.contrast: Auto-increment and auto-decrement also use a register as an address, but they step the register by the operand size instead of adding a fixed offset. Look for the constant in the address.

check.body: Check that the constant fits and that the other options fail. The offset 400 lies between $-32768$ and $32767$, so a signed 16-bit X can hold it. Using R1 alone as the address gives marks[0], which is 400 bytes before grade, so a mode that uses only R1 cannot reach it.

questions.stem: Consider a RISC machine where each instruction is exactly 4 bytes long. Conditional and unconditional branch instructions use PC-relative addressing mode with Offset specified in bytes to the target location of the branch instruction. Further the Offset is always with respect to the address of the next instruction in the program sequence. Consider the following instruction sequence. If the target of the branch instruction is i, then the decimal value of the Offset is ________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Four 4-byte instructions at i, i+4, i+8, i+12; the next PC is i+16, so a branch back to i has offset -16.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: PC-relative addressing computes a branch target as the program counter plus a signed offset stored in the instruction. By the time a branch executes, the PC has already moved on to the next instruction, so the rule given in the stem is: target = (address of next instruction) + Offset. A negative offset jumps backwards.

steps.title: Addresses
steps.body: Let instruction number $i$ sit at address $A$. Each instruction is 4 bytes, so beq (instruction $i+3$) is at $A+12$ and the next instruction is at $A+16$.

steps.title: Solve for the offset
steps.body: The target is instruction $i$, at address $A$. So $A=(A+16)+\text{Offset}$, which gives Offset $=-16$ bytes.

shortcut.body: Offset = target minus next instruction = go back 4 instructions of 4 bytes = $-16$. Thirty seconds. The common error is measuring from beq itself, which gives $-12$.

traps.text: Measuring from the address of beq instead of the next instruction gives $-12$. The stem states the offset is relative to the next instruction.
Writing +16 loses the sign. The target is behind the branch, so the offset is negative.
Counting in instructions rather than bytes gives $-4$. The stem says the offset is in bytes.

recognize.clues: The offset is stated to be in bytes and relative to the next instruction, with a fixed 4-byte instruction size and a branch that goes back to an earlier instruction.
recognize.contrast: Absolute branch addressing stores the target address itself. PC-relative stores only the distance, so the value depends on where the branch sits.

check.body: Replay the branch with numbers. Put i at address 100, so beq is at 112 and the next instruction is at 116. Adding the offset to 116 must land on 100, which tests both the sign and the unit.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: gate cse 2017 set 1 question 49
GATE 2017 CS session 1 final answer key (CS-1, IIT Roorkee, 16 Mar 2017), gatecse.in Google Drive copy

hints.text: Does the offset count from the branch itself or from the instruction after it? Write the address of each instruction in terms of the address of instruction i.
PC-relative addressing forms the target as the PC plus a signed offset, and a branch to an earlier instruction needs a negative offset.
When the offset is taken from the next instruction, offset equals the target address minus the address of that next instruction, measured in bytes.
Give instruction i the address A. Each instruction takes 4 bytes. Write the address of beq, then of the instruction after it, then subtract.
beq is the fourth instruction, so it sits 12 bytes after A. Now ask which instruction the offset is measured from.

variation.stem: Every instruction is exactly 8 bytes long, and a branch uses PC-relative addressing with its offset in bytes, taken from the address of the next instruction. A loop has instructions numbered j, j+1, j+2, j+3, j+4 and j+5, and the last one, j+5, is a branch whose target is instruction j+1. What is the decimal value of the Offset?
variation.explanation: Let j+1 sit at address B. Then the branch at j+5 is at B+32 and the next instruction is at B+40. The offset is the target minus the next instruction address, $B-(B+40)=-40$ bytes.
